idiom_name: DispatchSourceTimer deadline re-armed on arrival (or AsyncTimerSequence + ContinuousClock in structured concurrency)
implementation_notes: The platform owns the timer: a DispatchSourceTimer on a dedicated queue is scheduled with a one-shot deadline and re-scheduled further into the future on every arrival, and its event handler is the absence alarm; DispatchTime is monotonic, so clock changes do not disturb the deadline. In Swift Concurrency the same pattern is a task racing arrivals against AsyncTimerSequence (swift-async-algorithms) or a ContinuousClock sleep, which gives a monotonic, injectable clock (SuspendingClock/ContinuousClock in tests) and keeps the monitor inside its parent task's lifetime. What remains hand-written is the per-subject expectation, the alert state machine and the escalation.
pitfalls: A DispatchSourceTimer must be resumed exactly once before release and must not be released while suspended (that traps); re-scheduling a suspended source is silently ignored, so always arm after resume().

Foundation's Timer on the run loop and Dispatch timers use different scheduling semantics: forgetting the leeway/tolerance makes the monitor wake at exactly the deadline and burn power on mobile and edge devices - set an explicit leeway.
Date-based bookkeeping is wall-clock: a user or NTP changing the system time yields negative or enormous 'silence'. Use DispatchTime, ContinuousClock or SuspendingClock for the budget.

Under strict concurrency (Swift 6) the timer's event handler is @Sendable: mutable last-seen state must live in an actor or an atomic, and jumping back to the main actor to publish an alert can be delayed by a busy UI.
